images.filename: Awaiting mr. Mladić in The Hague (1).jpg
images.caption: Press cars lined up opposite an entrance of Scheveningen prison on the day a court session took place in Belgrade concerning the handover of Ratko Mladić to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. His lawyer's appeal was rejected the following day, and mr. Mladić was transferred to Scheveningen that same day.

images.caption:
Since its establishment, it was the Tribunal’s goal for the proceedings to be public and transparent while conducted in accordance with the highest international human rights standards, respecting both the rights of the accused and the dignity of all other participants in the proceedings, primarily the witnesses. 

When the Tribunal was established in 1993, most national jurisdictions did not broadcast criminal trials nor a need to translate their proceedings into two languages, let alone four. Thanks to its state-of-the-art courtroom technology, the Tribunal is able to bring its proceedings in The Hague to the people of the former Yugoslavia and to the world.

images.caption: Over the last 23 years, thousands of visitors to the ICTY have attended public hearings. At its peak, the Tribunal had three courtrooms and up to 7 trials were held on a day. The trials were held in either the morning session or the afternoon session so two trials a days could be held in each courtroom.

images.caption: The Tribunal’s audio visual archive holds more than 60,000 hours of public court proceedings. In 2010, the Tribunal undertook a project to digitize its recordings of hearings from tapes, which were subject to deterioration over time. The digitisation preserved these valuable recordings and facilitated future public access to the Tribunal’s hearings, maintaining transparency even after the culmination of the ICTY’s functioning.
